groups.name: Volcanic silica
groups.why: Silica filled the gas pockets and cracks of the same lava and ash.
groups.means: Silica-rich water filled the gas pockets, cracks and hollows of rhyolite and welded tuff. Agate, jasper and opal grew there, and the same filling makes a thunderegg's core; obsidian is that lava cooled to glass. Precious opal at Spencer sits in common opal in the gas cavities of a rhyolite-obsidian flow.
groups.expect: Hard, glassy to waxy pieces weathering out on the slopes and washing into the creeks below; thundereggs "weather out of the rhyolites" (Mason 1952).
groups.srcs: Staples 1965, Ore Bin 27(10); Mason 1952, Ore Bin 14(7); USBM 1995, SP 14-95

groups.name: Mica-beryl pegmatite
groups.why: They crystallise together in the same coarse granite veins.
groups.means: Pegmatite: very coarse granite in veins and pods, where the last of the melt grew big crystals. Mica books, black tourmaline (schorl), garnet and beryl crystallise together in it.
groups.expect: Find the pegmatite first: very coarse white quartz and feldspar with shiny mica. The other stones sit in it or loose in the soil and rubble below it.
groups.srcs: Stoll 1950, USGS PP 229 p.3, p.19; Bradley and McCauley 2013, USGS OF 2013-1008

groups.name: Gas-pocket pegmatite
groups.why: They grow in the open pockets of the same granite.
groups.means: Gas pockets (miarolitic cavities) in granite, where crystals grew freely into open space: smoky quartz, topaz and aquamarine together, as in Idaho's Sawtooth batholith.
groups.expect: Free-grown crystals with flat faces, in the pockets or in the gravel and soil below pocket-bearing granite. Smoky quartz is the most common; topaz and aquamarine are the prizes.
groups.srcs: Boggs 1985, GSA Abstracts 17; Foley et al. 2017, USGS PP 1802-E

groups.name: Mine dumps
groups.why: Ore and its weathered crust from the same veins.
groups.src: Cox 1986, USGS B 1693; Ransome and Calkins 1908
groups.means: Metal veins and their weathered tops. Galena, pyrite and rhodochrosite grew in the vein; where it weathered near the surface, native silver, pyromorphite and the green and blue copper carbonates (malachite, azurite) formed from them.
groups.expect: On the old dumps: heavy grey galena, brassy pyrite, pink rhodochrosite; green and blue crusts in the rusty, weathered rock (copper carbonates are "found sparingly", Ransome and Calkins). Dumps are often on claims or private land: ask first.
groups.srcs: Cox 1986, USGS B 1693 model 22c; Ransome and Calkins 1908, USGS PP 62 p.111; Pardee 1918, USGS B 690-E

groups.name: River gravel gems
groups.why: Heavy stones settle out in the same gravel.
groups.means: Heavy stones settle together in river gravel even though they came from different rocks: sapphire from volcanic rock, garnet from schist and gneiss.
groups.expect: Small rounded or broken pieces at the bottom of the gravel, best found by screening and panning the heavy part; gold and magnetite turn up in the same pan (Berg 2007).
groups.srcs: Clabaugh 1952, USGS B 983 p.29-30; Berg 2007, MBMG B 134; Berg and Landry 2018, MBMG B 136

groups.name: Skarn
groups.why: Granite baked limestone into the same contact rock.
groups.means: Skarn: where granite baked limestone, the contact grew grossular-andradite garnet and epidote, with magnetite and specular hematite, and copper ore that weathers to malachite and azurite (the Empire mine near Mackay, Idaho).
groups.expect: Garnet-rich rock right at the granite-limestone contact, shiny black specular hematite, and green and blue copper stains where the ore weathered.
groups.srcs: Farwell and Full 1944, USGS OF 44-17; Cox and Theodore 1986, USGS B 1693 models 18b, 18d
